ans-exam-overview-diagram-1.section: The four domains and where they live in this course
ans-exam-overview-diagram-1.caption: The four content domains with their weightings. Network Design and Network Implementation together make up more than half of the scored content.
notes: 1. Domain 1: Network Design (30%): Edge, DNS, load balancing, logging requirements, hybrid and multi-account routing strategy (6 tasks).
2. Domain 2: Network Implementation (26%): Build hybrid links, multi-account connectivity, hybrid DNS and automation (4 tasks).
3. Domain 3: Management and Operation (20%): Maintain routing, monitor and troubleshoot, optimize cost and performance (3 tasks).
4. Domain 4: Security, Compliance, Governance (24%): Secure flows, audit with logs, protect data in transit (3 tasks).

ans-exam-overview-diagram-2.caption: A suggested eight-week rhythm. Each loop is read, build, verify, then drill questions on that domain.
notes: 1. Foundations: Week 1: OSI, CIDR, BGP, MTU, VPC
3. Hybrid + multi-VPC: Weeks 4 to 5, the heaviest

network-foundations-diagram-1.section: The OSI layers you must be able to use
network-foundations-diagram-1.caption: OSI layers with typical AWS services. Higher layers can inspect more but add latency and cost.
notes: 1. L7 Application: HTTP, gRPC, DNS. ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AWS WAF, Route 53.
2. L6 / L5 Presentation, session: TLS termination and sessions. ALB and NLB TLS listeners, ACM certificates.
3. L4 Transport: TCP, UDP ports. NLB, security groups, network ACLs, NAT gateway, Global Accelerator.
4. L3 Network: IP, ICMP, routing, BGP. Route tables, Transit Gateway, GWLB (GENEVE), VPN (IPsec).
5. L2 Data link: Ethernet, VLAN 802.1Q, LAG, MACsec. Direct Connect VIFs ride a VLAN.
6. L1 Physical: Fibre, optics, cross-connects. Direct Connect location, LOA-CFA.

network-foundations-diagram-2.section: Routing: longest prefix, static and BGP
network-foundations-diagram-2.caption: Longest prefix match. The /24 wins for 10.1.1.5 even though the /16 also matches; 10.1.9.9 only matches the /16.

network-foundations-diagram-3.section: How a VPC forwards a packet
network-foundations-diagram-3.caption: Packet path from an instance to a remote VPC. A block at any step stops the flow.
notes: Next hop: TGW, IGW, PCX, VGW

cloudfront-design-diagram-1.caption: Cache hierarchy. A hit at the edge never touches the origin; Origin Shield adds one more consolidating cache in front of the origin.
notes: Edge location: cache hit returns here
Edge location → Regional edge cache: miss
Regional edge cache → Origin Shield: miss

cloudfront-design-diagram-2.caption: Protecting each origin type. Each layer removes the direct-to-origin path.
notes: 1. S3 origin: Origin access control (OAC): bucket policy allows only the CloudFront service principal for that distribution. Block public access stays on.
2. ALB / NLB / EC2 in private subnets: CloudFront VPC origins keep the origin private with no public IP, reached through a service-managed ENI.
3. Public ALB or custom origin: Allow the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront origin-facing IPs in the security group, plus a secret custom header the origin verifies (rotate it).
4. API Gateway: Use an edge-optimized or regional endpoint with a CloudFront-added header or API key; resource policy or WAF for validation.
5. Viewer side: HTTPS only (redirect HTTP), TLS 1.2+ security policy, AWS WAF web ACL attached to the distribution.

global-accelerator-edge-diagram-1.caption: Global Accelerator structure. Listeners accept TCP or UDP on chosen ports; each listener routes to endpoint groups (one per Region) containing endpoints.
notes: Endpoint group us-east-1 → ALB / NLB / EC2 / EIP
Endpoint group eu-west-1 → ALB / NLB / EC2 / EIP

route53-public-private-diagram-1.caption: Split-horizon DNS. The same name can resolve differently inside the VPC (PHZ) and outside (public zone).
notes: Instance in VPC → Private hosted zone: VPC resolver
Internet user → Public hosted zone: public resolvers

route53-routing-health-diagram-1.caption: Choosing between the policies by what you need to control. Position is approximate.
notes: Horizontal axis: User location awareness; vertical axis: Control over traffic share
Simple: lower User location awareness; lower Control over traffic share
Multivalue: lower User location awareness; lower Control over traffic share
Weighted: lower User location awareness; higher Control over traffic share
Failover: lower User location awareness; higher Control over traffic share
Latency: higher User location awareness; lower Control over traffic share
Geolocation: higher User location awareness; lower Control over traffic share
Geoproximity: higher User location awareness; higher Control over traffic share

route53-routing-health-diagram-2.caption: Active/passive failover. Route 53 returns the primary while it is healthy; when it fails, the secondary record is returned.

hybrid-dns-resolver-diagram-1.caption: Hybrid DNS with both endpoint types. On-premises forwards aws.example.com to the inbound endpoint; the VPC forwards corp.example.com to the outbound endpoint.
notes: On-prem DNS servers → Inbound endpoint: aws.example.com
Outbound endpoint → On-prem DNS servers: forward rule (dashed connection)
VPC Resolver → Outbound endpoint: conditional forwarding rule

dnssec-dns-security-diagram-1.caption: Chain of trust. The parent zone holds a DS record that vouches for the child zone's key-signing key.
notes: 1. Root zone: Trust anchor in validating resolvers
3. example.com (child): KSK signs the ZSK; ZSK signs record sets (RRSIG)
4. Validating resolver: Checks signatures up the chain

elb-types-layers-diagram-1.caption: Which load balancer works at which layer. The Classic Load Balancer is legacy and is rarely the right answer on the exam.
notes: Application Load Balancer: Layer 7: HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket
Network Load Balancer: Layer 4: TCP, UDP, TLS
Gateway Load Balancer: Layer 3 gateway + L4 balancing, GENEVE

elb-types-layers-diagram-2.caption: Static IPs with Layer 7 routing. An NLB with Elastic IPs forwards to an ALB target group, which applies host and path rules.

elb-config-integration-diagram-1.caption: Three TLS designs. Choose by whether the load balancer must see the content, and by compliance needs.
notes: 1. TLS termination: Client TLS to ALB/NLB with an ACM certificate; plain HTTP to targets inside the VPC. Offloads CPU and enables layer 7 features.
2. Re-encryption (end to end): Terminate at ALB, then new TLS session to targets. Required where compliance forbids clear text inside the VPC. Target certificates need not be public CA issued.
3. TLS passthrough: NLB TCP listener forwards encrypted bytes untouched; target holds the certificate. The load balancer cannot inspect HTTP, and the client IP is preserved.

elb-config-integration-diagram-2.caption: A typical internet application: global DNS and edge, a WAF-protected ALB, and an Auto Scaling group across two AZs.

direct-connect-design-diagram-1.caption: Physical path. Your router connects by cross connect to an AWS DX router in a colocation facility; AWS carries the traffic over its backbone to the Region.
notes: Customer router → Cross connect: carrier / own fibre (dashed connection)
AWS DX router → AWS Region: AWS backbone

direct-connect-design-diagram-2.caption: Maximum resiliency: two DX locations, each with two connections to two separate on-premises routers. Active BGP sessions run over all four.

direct-connect-implementation-diagram-1.caption: Two VIF types sharing a physical connection. The private VIF reaches a VPC; the public VIF reaches AWS public services such as S3 without the internet.
notes: DX connection: VLAN 101 private, VLAN 102 public
DX connection → Public VIF → AWS public services

direct-connect-implementation-diagram-2.caption: Transit VIF design. One DX gateway reaches Transit Gateways in two Regions, each connected to many VPCs.
notes: On-premises → Direct Connect gateway: transit VIF

site-to-site-client-vpn-diagram-1.caption: Two tunnels per connection. Configure both on the customer device; one active and one standby, or both active with ECMP on a Transit Gateway.
notes: Customer gateway device: public IP, ASN

bgp-routing-policy-diagram-1.caption: Traffic engineering levers, strongest first. Prefix length beats all attributes; local preference is the main outbound control.
notes: 1. Longest prefix: /25 beats /24 regardless of attributes
2. Local preference: Highest wins; local to your AS
3. AS_PATH length: Shortest wins; prepend to de-prefer
4. MED: Lowest wins; hints to a neighbour
5. Other tie-breakers: eBGP over iBGP, router ID

bgp-routing-policy-diagram-2.caption: Active/passive over two Direct Connect locations using local preference communities. Traffic from AWS prefers DX-1; DX-2 takes over if the primary BGP session drops.
notes: AWS (VGW / DXGW) → DX-2 standby: backup (dashed connection)

hybrid-sdwan-redundancy-diagram-1.caption: Direct Connect primary with VPN backup into a Transit Gateway. The DXGW route is preferred; if it drops, the VPN route takes over automatically through BGP.

hybrid-sdwan-redundancy-diagram-2.caption: SD-WAN with Transit Gateway Connect. GRE+BGP rides on a VPC attachment as transport; branch sites reach VPCs through the overlay.
notes: Branch SD-WAN edges → SD-WAN appliance: overlay (dashed connection)
SD-WAN appliance → Transit Gateway: GRE + BGP

vpc-design-addressing-diagram-1.caption: A three-tier VPC across two AZs. NAT gateways are per AZ so a zone failure does not break egress for the other zone.

vpc-peering-vs-tgw-diagram-1.caption: Transitivity trap. A reaches B and B reaches C, but A cannot reach C unless it has its own peering (or a transit gateway).
notes: VPC A → VPC C: no path (dashed connection)

transit-gateway-architectures-diagram-1.caption: Prod and dev VPCs are isolated from each other but both reach shared services and on-premises. Each spoke associates with its own route table; the shared and on-premises attachments propagate into both.
notes: DX gateway to on-premises: assoc: RT-Shared
Transit Gateway ↔ DX gateway to on-premises

privatelink-endpoints-diagram-1.caption: Gateway endpoint adds a route; interface endpoint adds an ENI. Only the interface endpoint is reachable from outside the VPC.
notes: Private subnet instance → Interface endpoint ENI
Interface endpoint ENI → AWS service / PrivateLink service

privatelink-endpoints-diagram-2.caption: PrivateLink provider and consumer. Many consumer VPCs reach one NLB-backed service without exposing the provider network.

vpc-sharing-organizations-diagram-1.caption: One network account owns the VPC and shares subnets; app teams in other accounts deploy into them and keep their own billing and IAM boundaries.
notes: Network account: owns VPC and subnets
App account A: launches in subnet-a
App account B: launches in subnet-b

network-monitoring-cloudwatch-diagram-1.caption: Monitoring design loop. Requirements decide which metrics, logs and alarms you need, and the baseline gives the alarms meaning.
notes: 2. Metrics + logs: Pick sources per service

flow-logs-traffic-mirroring-diagram-1.caption: Traffic mirroring. A session links a source ENI, a filter and a target; the monitoring appliance receives VXLAN copies without affecting production traffic.

reachability-network-manager-diagram-1.caption: Analysis workflow. Create a path, run an analysis, read the explanation, fix the component, rerun.
notes: 1. Define path: Source, destination, protocol, port
2. Run analysis: Control-plane model, no traffic
3. Read result: Hops or blocking component
4. Fix + rerun: Route, SG, NACL, attachment

network-automation-iac-diagram-1.caption: Self-healing and guardrail pattern. A risky change is detected, evaluated and reverted or escalated automatically.

maintaining-routing-quotas-diagram-1.caption: Route maintenance loop. Every change should be reviewed, tested and monitored.
notes: 4. Monitor: Blackhole, drop and BGP alarms

troubleshooting-playbook-diagram-1.caption: Work from the bottom up or divide in half. Each step uses a specific tool, so you eliminate layers rather than guess.
notes: 1. Define the flow: Source, destination, port, protocol, direction
3. Route: Route tables, TGW, Reachability Analyzer
4. Filters: SG, NACL, firewall, flow logs REJECT
5. Path quality: MTU, loss, latency, asymmetry

performance-cost-optimization-diagram-1.caption: Ways to cut bandwidth and latency, from the application outward.
notes: 1. Application: Compression, protocol efficiency, batching, HTTP/2 and keep-alive
2. Edge: CloudFront caching, Global Accelerator for better paths
3. Placement: Same AZ for chatty tiers, cluster placement groups, ENA Express
4. Frames: Jumbo frames end to end, tuned MSS
5. Replication: Multicast for one-to-many instead of repeated unicast

threat-modeling-inbound-security-diagram.caption: Layered inbound defence. Each layer removes a class of attack before it reaches the next.
notes: 1. DNS and edge: Route 53 (Shield protected), CloudFront or Global Accelerator absorb floods; geo-restrictions
2. AWS WAF + Shield: Layer 7 rules, rate limits, bot control; Shield Advanced adds DDoS response team and cost protection
3. Load balancer in public subnets: TLS termination, ALB only in the perimeter, security group allows CloudFront prefix list or required ports
4. Application tier in private subnets: No public IPs; SG allows only the ALB security group
5. Data tier in isolated subnets: SG allows only the application SG; no internet route

threat-modeling-inbound-security-diagram.caption: Perimeter (DMZ) VPC pattern. Untrusted traffic terminates in a perimeter VPC where WAF, firewall and reverse proxies live; only inspected traffic crosses Transit Gateway to private workload VPCs.

outbound-inspection-firewall-diagram-1.caption: Centralized inspection with Transit Gateway. Spoke route tables send 0.0.0.0/0 to the inspection attachment; the inspection VPC sends cleaned traffic to the egress NAT or back to another spoke.

sg-nacl-firewall-manager-audit-diagram-1.caption: Firewall Manager flow. The administrator defines a policy and scope; Config detects resources; non-compliant resources are reported or auto-remediated in member accounts.
notes: 1. Define policy: Type, scope (OUs, tags), remediation
3. Apply / remediate: Create or fix resources in member accounts

encryption-in-transit-certificates-diagr.caption: Encryption options along the path from user to data. A compliant design names the control for every segment.
notes: 1. User to edge: HTTPS with CloudFront (TLS 1.2+/1.3), viewer protocol policy redirect-to-HTTPS, HSTS
2. Edge to origin: Origin protocol policy HTTPS only; valid cert on ALB/NLB; match host header
3. Load balancer to targets: Re-encrypt with HTTPS/TLS target groups, or NLB TCP passthrough
4. Between instances / VPCs: Nitro instances encrypt traffic between supported instance types automatically; TLS/mTLS in the application; TGW and inter-Region peering encrypt at the physical layer
5. On-premises to AWS: IPsec Site-to-Site VPN; IPsec over Direct Connect (public VIF or private IP VPN on transit VIF); MACsec on the DX link
6. To AWS services: TLS endpoints for S3 (enforce aws:SecureTransport), RDS SSL/TLS, DynamoDB, KMS

scenario-global-application-diagram-1.section: A design that satisfies every requirement
scenario-global-application-diagram-1.caption: Reference design. Storefront and API use different edge services because they have different protocol and addressing requirements.
notes: CloudFront + WAF: OAC for S3 assets
Global Accelerator: 2 static IPs, TCP port

scenario-enterprise-hybrid-diagram-1.caption: Landing zone network. A dedicated Network account owns the Transit Gateways, Direct Connect gateway, inspection VPC and DNS; workload accounts attach through RAM-shared Transit Gateways.
notes: Direct Connect gateway: transit VIFs, 2 locations
Inspection VPC: Network Firewall, appliance mode
TGW us-east-1 ↔ TGW eu-west-1: TGW peering

lab-hub-spoke-transit-gateway-diagram-1.caption: Lab topology. Each spoke associates with its own TGW route table and learns only the shared VPC route.

exam-technique-and-review-diagram-1.caption: A four-pass method for scenario questions. The constraint words decide the answer, not the services you recognise.
notes: 1. Ask: Read the last sentence first: what must I choose?
2. Constraints: Underline cost, time, scale, security, minimal change
3. Eliminate: Cross out options that break any constraint
4. Choose: Pick the simplest option that satisfies all

network-automation-iac-diagram-2.caption: Automation for cost and hygiene
notes: 1. Detect: Cost Explorer, Trusted Advisor, Config, Flow Logs
2. Decide: Idle NAT, unattached EIP, oversized links, stale endpoints
3. Act: Scheduled Lambda/SSM or IaC change via pipeline

lab-hub-spoke-transit-gateway-diagram-2.caption: Build the network
notes: 1. VPCs + subnets: 3 VPCs, one private subnet each
